messages.content:
<question>
The landlord of my apartment in Colombia failed to do an indispensable repair (not a minor one), and I paid COP 2,000,000 for it myself. Our contract says nothing about deductions and my rent is COP 1,200,000. If I am entitled to recover the cost from the rent, what is the most I can deduct each month and how many months will it take?
</question>

<answer>
In Dubai, a tenant who pays for an indispensable repair that the landlord failed to carry out may recover the cost by deducting it from the rent. Each monthly deduction may not exceed 50% of the rent. The tenant may continue making deductions in successive months until the full cost has been recovered. If the tenancy ends before the cost is recovered, the tenant may keep the premises until the unpaid balance is settled.
</answer>

<reference>
Unless the parties agreed otherwise, in the case art. 27 refers to (art. 1993 of the Civil Code, which the corpus does not include) the tenant may deduct the cost of indispensable non-locative repairs from the rent, but never more than 30% of the rent: 30% x 1,200,000 = COP 360,000 a month. Because the total exceeds that amount, the tenant may make periodic deductions of up to 30% of the rent until the whole cost is recovered: 2,000,000 / 360,000 = 5.6, so five deductions of COP 360,000 (1,800,000) and a sixth of COP 200,000, six months in all. If the contract ends before the cost is recovered, the tenant may exercise the right of retention until the landlord has paid the unpaid balance in full (art. 27, last paragraph, and art. 26 of Ley 820 de 2003). Whether the conditions of the Civil Code article are met is not something the corpus can settle.
</reference>

First write your reasoning, then give the verdict, pass or fail.

The criterion is correctness against a reference answer that a person checked against the statute. The answer passes if it states the same rule as the reference on what the question asks: the same obligation, right, period, amount, condition or exception that the reference relies on. Extra correct detail is fine. Leaving out a condition or exception that the reference treats as essential fails, and so does any statement that contradicts the reference. Wording, order and length do not matter. If the reference says part of the question cannot be answered from the law, the answer must leave that part open too, not fill it in.

In your reasoning, name the rule the reference states, then say whether the answer states it, leaves part of it out, or contradicts it.

The reference states the rule: the tenant may deduct the cost of indispensable non-locative repairs from rent, capped at 30% of rent per month (COP 360,000), with periodic deductions until recovered, giving six months (five of 360,000 and one of 200,000), and a right of retention if the contract ends before recovery. The answer instead discusses Dubai law, states a 50% cap rather than 30%, and does not address Colombia at all. The jurisdiction is wrong and the cap contradicts the reference's 30% figure. It also omits the Colombian monthly figure and timing. The answer therefore contradicts the reference on the key amount and fails to state the governing rule.","verdict":"fail"}
